entry: Branch of philosophy that studies the nature of language and its relation to meaning, reference and the world. Investigations include the nature of meaning, indexicality, intentionality, reference and the constitution of sentences. Inquiry dates to ancient Greece, where [[Plato]] asked in the dialogue *Cratylus* whether names are conventional or natural. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, [[Gottlob Frege]] and [[Bertrand Russell]] were pivotal figures in analytic philosophy's linguistic turn, followed by [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]] in *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus*. His later *Philosophical Investigations* (1953) stressed language as embedded in practical use. Major subfields include [[Semantics]], which studies truth-conditional meaning, and [[Pragmatics]], which examines how context and speaker intentions shape interpretation.

Branch of philosophy concerned with the nature of mathematics and its relation to epistemology and metaphysics. Central questions include whether mathematical objects are purely abstract or in some way concrete, and how they relate to physical reality. Paradoxes discovered around the end of the 19th century, including [[Russell's paradox]], made the logical foundations of mathematics questionable. The study of infinite sets by [[Georg Cantor]] led to the idea of several sizes of infinity. [[Gottlob Frege]] and [[Bertrand Russell]] championed logicism, which holds that mathematics derives from logic, while [[David Hilbert]] treated mathematics as a formal system of symbols manipulated by syntactic rules. Later work in [[Mathematical logic]] provided a framework in which theorems follow from axioms by inference rules.

Branch of philosophy concerned with the nature of the mind and its relation to the body and the external world. Its central issue is the mind–body problem, and it also addresses the hard problem of consciousness and the nature of particular mental states. Dualism entered Western philosophy through [[René Descartes]] in the 17th century, who held that the mind is an independent substance. [[Baruch Spinoza]] instead held that mind and body are properties of one underlying substance. Most modern philosophers hold that the mind is not separate from the body, and [[Behaviorism]] is one physicalist position. Questions about how subjective experience and intentionality can be explained in naturalistic terms remain unresolved, and the field has strong ties to [[Neuroscience]] and [[Artificial intelligence]].

Branch of philosophy that critically examines the central themes and concepts of religious traditions, such as God, souls, miracles and salvation. It differs from [[Theology]] by evaluating the logical coherence and truth of religious concepts independently of any particular tradition, and from [[Religious studies]] by not being limited to historical or sociological perspectives. The field overlaps with [[Metaphysics]], epistemology, logic, ethics and aesthetics. Philosophical discussions of religion appear in ancient texts, including the Hindu [[Upanishads]], and [[Stoicism]] included theories of deities, while [[Aristotle]] described an unmoved mover in his metaphysics. [[Medieval philosophy]] was strongly shaped by the Abrahamic religions. The term came into general use in the West only in the 19th century. Classic topics include the existence of God, the problem of evil and [[Miracle|miracles]].

Branch of philosophy concerned with the foundations, methods and implications of science. Central questions include the difference between science and non-science, whether science can infer truth about unobservable entities, and whether inductive reasoning can justify definite knowledge. [[Francis Bacon]] advocated systematic empirical methods in the 17th century, but the field emerged as a distinct discipline only in the 20th century, after the [[Positivism|logical positivist]] movement. [[Karl Popper]] criticized logical positivism and helped establish modern standards of scientific methodology. Thomas Kuhn's *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions* (1962) argued that scientific progress is relative to a paradigm, the set of questions, concepts and practices that define a discipline in a given period. Paul Feyerabend and others argued against the existence of a single scientific method.

American animated musical-comedy television series. Created by Dan Povenmire and Jeff Marsh for [[Disney Channel]], it follows stepbrothers Phineas Flynn and Ferb Fletcher, who build elaborate projects during their summer vacation while Phineas's older sister Candace tries to expose them to their mother. Their secret agent pet, [[Platypus|Perry the Platypus]], thwarts the schemes of Dr. Heinz Doofenshmirtz. The series originally aired from 2007 to 2015 and returned in 2025. Povenmire and Marsh pitched it to networks for 16 years before selling it to [[The Walt Disney Company]].

Form of social engineering in which attackers deceive people into revealing sensitive information or installing [[Malware|malware]]. Phishing often arrives by [[Email|email]] or [[SMS|text message]] and may redirect victims to a counterfeit login page that collects credentials. Spear phishing targets particular individuals, and whaling targets senior leaders. Voice phishing, or vishing, uses telephone calls, and some attacks relay [[Authentication|authentication]] to a legitimate site to capture sessions. Phishing is a common initial-access method, and [[Large language model|large language models]] can automate personalized lures at low cost. In one field experiment, 43% of participants clicked at least one simulated phishing link.

Capital and most populous city of [[Cambodia]], at the confluence of the Tonlé Sap and [[Mekong]] rivers. It regained capital status during the French colonial era and is the seat of Cambodia's monarchy at the Royal Palace. The city was founded in 1372 and was the national capital from 1434 until 1497, after the fall of Angkor. Its name derives from Wat Phnom, a Buddhist temple, and Lady Penh, the city's founder. Known as the Pearl of Asia for its French colonial, New Khmer and [[Art Deco]] architecture, it was forcibly evacuated in 1975 by the [[Khmer Rouge]], and it remained largely uninhabited until Vietnam-backed forces took it in 1979. By 2009 it had more than 2 million people, approximately 14% of the Cambodian population.

[[Vietnam|Vietnamese]] noodle soup dish of broth, rice noodles, herbs and usually [[Beef|beef]] or chicken. It first appeared in written records in the early 20th century in northern Vietnam, and the modern form emerged between 1900 and 1907 in Nam Định Province. Beef consumption was not widespread because [[Water buffalo|water buffaloes]] were used for farming, and the origins of pho remain debated, with possible French and Chinese influences. Refugees popularized pho worldwide after the [[Vietnam War]]. The Hanoi and Saigon styles differ in noodle width, broth sweetness and choice of herbs. In 2017 Vietnam made December 12 the Day of Pho.

[[Anxiety disorder]] characterized by a persistent, irrational and excessive fear of an object or situation. Phobias typically arise with rapid onset of fear and are usually present for more than six months. Sufferers go to great lengths to avoid the feared object or situation, to a degree greater than the actual danger posed. Phobias are divided into specific phobias, social anxiety disorder and [[Agoraphobia|agoraphobia]]. The most common specific phobias involve spiders, cockroaches, snakes and heights. Specific phobias affect about 6–8% of people in the [[Western world]] in a given year, and women are affected about twice as often as men. Specific phobias are usually treated with exposure therapy. Medications are not helpful for specific phobias. Social phobia and agoraphobia may be treated with counseling and medication such as antidepressants or [[Benzodiazepine|benzodiazepines]]. People with phobias are more likely to attempt [[Suicide|suicide]].

Larger and innermost of the two moons of [[Mars]]. Discovered in 1877 by Asaph Hall, it is a small, irregular body with a mean radius of 11 km that orbits about 6,000 km above the Martian surface. It completes an orbit in 7 hours and 39 minutes, faster than Mars rotates. It is one of the least reflective bodies in the Solar System, and its surface is marked by the large [[Impact crater|impact crater]] Stickney. Named after the Greek god of fear and panic, it is the twin brother of [[Deimos (moon)|Deimos]].

Consonantal writing system (an abjad) used in [[Phoenicia]] and across the Mediterranean from c. 1050 to 146 BC. It was one of the first alphabets and the first to have a fixed writing direction, written horizontally from right to left. It developed from the Proto-Sinaitic script of the Late Bronze Age, which derived in turn from [[Egyptian hieroglyphs]]. Its 22 consonant letters left vowels implicit, though late varieties sometimes used matres lectionis to mark some vowels. Phoenician merchants spread it across the Mediterranean, and its descendants include the Aramaic and Samaritan alphabets and the [[Greek alphabet|Archaic Greek alphabets]]. Because each sound had its own symbol, it needed only a few dozen signs, far fewer than [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] or hieroglyphic writing, which required long training. The alphabet proper was used in [[Carthage]] until the 2nd century BC.

Capital and most populous city of [[Arizona]], U.S. With over 1.6 million residents at the 2020 census, it is the fifth-most populous city in the United States and the most populous state capital. It lies in the Salt River Valley, with a [[Desert climate|hot desert climate]]. Settled in 1867 as an agricultural community, it was incorporated in 1881 and became capital of the Arizona Territory in 1889. Irrigation canals built by earlier Hohokam people were reused, and the local economy long depended on [[Cotton|cotton]], [[Cattle|cattle]], citrus, climate and [[Copper|copper]], known locally as the Five C's. High-tech companies arrived after [[World War II]], when [[Air conditioning|air conditioning]] made summers more bearable. Hispanic residents make up 42% of the population.

Marine protected area in central [[Kiribati]], an ocean nation approximately midway between [[Australia]] and [[Hawaii]]. It covers 408,250 sq km (157,630 sq mi), about 11.34% of Kiribati's exclusive economic zone, and is one of the largest marine protected areas and one of the largest protected areas of any type on Earth. Designated in 2010 as the world's largest and deepest [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]], it conserves one of the world's largest intact oceanic coral archipelago ecosystems, including 14 underwater [[Seamount|seamounts]] and approximately 800 known species of fauna. Commercial extractive activities, including [[Tuna|tuna]] fishing, were prohibited throughout the area from January 1, 2015. In November 2021 the government announced it would end protection to boost tuna fishing, and the area reopened to commercial fishing in 2023.

Legendary immortal bird that cyclically regenerates or is born again, rising from the ashes of its predecessor. It originated in [[Greek mythology]] and has analogues in many cultures, including Egyptian and Persian mythology. Associated with the [[Sun|sun]], the phoenix was said in some legends to die in flames and in others to burn and decompose before being reborn. [[Herodotus]], writing in the 5th century BC, attributed its origin to [[Ancient Egypt]], reporting an account of a bird that came to Heliopolis once in five hundred years. Later writers, including [[Ovid]] and [[Pliny the Elder]], linked the phoenix to renewal, the [[Roman Empire]] and resurrection. The Greek word is first attested in Mycenaean Greek, where it probably meant griffin, though it might have meant palm tree.

Family of [[Spider|spiders]] with more than 2,000 species, including the cellar spider and the daddy long-legs spider. First described by Carl Ludwig Koch in 1850, pholcids have extremely long, thin legs, and most have eight eyes in two groups of three. They occur on every continent except [[Antarctica]], hanging upside down in messy, irregular webs in caves, under bark and in buildings such as cellars and attics. Their webs have no adhesive, so they rely on tangled structure and wrap prey in silk. When disturbed, some species vibrate their webs rapidly. The name daddy long-legs is also used for [[Opiliones|harvestmen]].

Basic unit of [[Phonology|phonology]], a set of speech sounds that speakers regard as a single sound distinguishing one word from another. All languages contain phonemes, and all spoken languages include both [[Consonant|consonant]] and [[Vowel|vowel]] phonemes. Written between slashes, as in /p/ and /b/, phonemes separate English words such as *pat* and *bat*. Phonemes are abstract, and the varying pronunciations of one phoneme are called allophones: the English /p/ is aspirated in *pit* but not in *spit*. Phonemes differ across languages, so [n] and [ŋ] are distinct in English, distinguishing *sin* and *sing*, but form one phoneme in Spanish. Linguists transcribe phonemes between slashes using the [[International Phonetic Alphabet]], and write precise pronunciations in square brackets, a distinction known as the difference between [[Phonetics|phonetic]] and phonemic transcription.

Branch of [[Linguistics|linguistics]] concerned with how humans produce and perceive speech sounds. It is traditionally divided into articulatory, acoustic and auditory phonetics, which study the articulation, sound-wave properties and perception of speech. Its minimal unit is the phone, an individual speech sound, whereas the [[Phoneme|phoneme]] is the abstract, language-specific unit that affects meaning. Phoneticians transcribe sounds with the [[International Phonetic Alphabet]], first published in 1888. The first known study of phonetics was undertaken by [[Sanskrit]] grammarians as early as the 6th century BCE, and the grammar of [[Pāṇini]], written c. 350 BCE, described principles including voicing. The term phonetics was first used in its present sense in 1841. The field also addresses [[Sign language|sign languages]], which are produced manually and perceived visually.

Genus of large [[Spider|spiders]] in the family Ctenidae, found mainly in northern South America, with one species in Central America. Members are commonly called Brazilian wandering spiders or banana spiders. Maximilian Perty named the genus in 1833, from the Greek for murderess. Leg spans reach 13 to 18 cm, and the defensive posture, with the front legs lifted high, is a distinctive sign. Their [[Venom|venom]] is neurotoxic, but fatalities are rare, and antivenom with supportive care manages most envenomations.

Device for the mechanical and analog reproduction of [[Sound|sound]], later called a gramophone. Sound is recorded as a groove on a rotating cylinder or disc. [[Thomas Edison]] invented the phonograph in 1877, and [[Alexander Graham Bell]]'s Volta Laboratory improved it in the 1880s. In the 1890s [[Emile Berliner]] moved to flat discs and coined the term gramophone. The disc record was the dominant commercial audio format for most of the 20th century. Use declined sharply in the 1980s as [[Cassette tape|cassettes]] and the [[Compact disc|compact disc]] became popular, but records have revived since the late 2000s.

Branch of linguistics concerned with how languages organize their basic sound elements. In spoken languages these are [[Phoneme|phonemes]], such as vowels and consonants that distinguish words like *bat* and *gnat*. In sign languages they include components such as hand shape and location. Phonology is distinguished from [[Phonetics]], which concerns the physical production, transmission and perception of sounds, and it also covers [[Syllable|syllables]], stress and intonation. The modern study of phonology was shaped by the 19th-century Polish scholar Jan Baudouin de Courtenay. In the mid-20th century [[Noam Chomsky]] and Morris Halle pioneered generative phonology, which derives surface forms from underlying representations by rules.

Anion, salt, functional group or ester derived from [[Phosphoric acid|phosphoric acid]]. Most often it means orthophosphate, the ion PO₄³⁻ formed by removing three protons from phosphoric acid. Sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and ammonium phosphates are water-soluble, while most others are only slightly soluble or insoluble. Orthophosphates are central to [[Biochemistry|biochemistry]] and ecology, since adding and removing phosphate groups is a key step in cell [[Metabolism|metabolism]], and phosphate groups form part of [[DNA]] and [[RNA]]. Mined worldwide, phosphates support plant growth as [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], but excess phosphate causes pollution and excessive plant growth.

Inorganic compound with the formula H₃PO₄, also called orthophosphoric acid. It is a colorless, odorless solid usually encountered as an 85% aqueous solution, and it is a major industrial chemical. Removing its three hydrogen ions gives the [[Phosphate]] ion PO₄³⁻, and it forms esters called organophosphates. The wet process, which treats phosphate minerals with [[Sulfuric acid|sulfuric acid]], accounts for over 90% of global output. The higher-purity thermal process burns [[Phosphorus|elemental phosphorus]] and dissolves the resulting oxide in water. Most output goes to [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], consuming about 80–90% of production. Concentrated phosphoric acid is highly corrosive, causing severe burns to skin, eyes and respiratory tissues, and it reacts violently with bases.

[[Chemical element]] with atomic number 15 and symbol P. Highly reactive, it is never found free in nature, and it makes up about 0.1% of Earth's crust, generally as phosphate rock. Its only stable isotope is ³¹P. The two most common allotropes are white phosphorus, which is highly toxic and glows as it oxidizes, and red phosphorus, used in matches and fire retardants. Hennig Brand of [[Hamburg]] isolated it in 1669, the first element discovered since antiquity. Phosphorus is essential to all known life through compounds such as [[DNA]], [[RNA]] and ATP. Most industrial production supports [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]]. In 2024 China, [[Morocco]], the United States and Russia were the leading producers of phosphate ore, and Morocco alone holds two-thirds of the estimated exploitable phosphate reserves.

Branch of [[Chemistry|chemistry]] concerned with the chemical effects of light. It usually describes reactions caused by absorption of [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] (wavelength 100 to 400 nm), visible (400–750 nm) or infrared (750–2500 nm) radiation. Photochemistry underlies [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], vision and the formation of [[Vitamin D|vitamin D]] in sunlight, but it also causes [[DNA|DNA]] mutations that lead to skin cancers. Photochemical paths reach high-energy intermediates that cannot be generated thermally. Its first law, the Grotthuss–Draper law, holds that light must be absorbed for a reaction to occur. The Stark–Einstein law, to which [[Albert Einstein]] contributed, holds that each absorbed photon activates no more than one molecule. Excited molecules can relax through [[Fluorescence|fluorescence]] or phosphorescence, and photodegradation can destroy plastics.
